The Last Light in Bellweather

Rain polished Bellweather's empty streets until every lamp had a twin beneath it. Mara Vale turned the sign on her bookshop door from OPEN to CLOSED, though the clock above the register had stopped at eleven minutes past nine three winters ago. She had never repaired it. Some endings deserved to remain visible.

She was carrying a stack of unsold hardcovers toward the back room when someone knocked. Elias Reed stood outside beneath a black umbrella, his gray coat shining at the shoulders. In one hand he held a small wooden box.

Mara unlocked the door. "You have five minutes before I become unreasonable."

"You were unreasonable when we were twenty," Elias said. "I assumed it was permanent."

He stepped inside, bringing rain and the faint metallic smell of the clockmaker's shop across the square. They had not spoken in six years, not since Mara's father died and Elias left for London the morning after the funeral.

Mara set the books down harder than necessary. "Four minutes."

Elias placed the box on the counter. Inside lay a brass key, dark with age, and a folded page covered in her father's narrow handwriting.

"He gave this to me before he died," Elias said. "He made me promise not to bring it back until the town clock stopped."

Outside, the great clock in Bellweather Tower struck ten. The first note rolled through the glass. The second never came.

Silence settled over the square.

Mara looked from the tower to Elias. "That is an unpleasantly theatrical coincidence."

"Your father enjoyed those."

She unfolded the page. It contained no farewell, only directions: beneath the western stair, behind the stone carved with a moth. Bring the key. Bring someone you once trusted.

"He knew we would fall out," Mara said.

"He knew you," Elias replied. "I was easier to predict."

The dead clock above the register clicked, and its minute hand moved forward once.

Mara closed her fingers around the brass key. "The tower will be locked."

Elias opened the umbrella. "Good thing we have a key."

She switched off the bookshop lights and stepped into the rain with him. Across the square, the dark face of Bellweather Tower waited.
